title: The dice-master's last day
hookLine: the patient brother faces Shalya, and the dice-master meets Sahadeva
carry: dharma is restored, in its own time
tomorrow: the last king is alone. where does he go?

cards: Who should face Shalya? On the Pandava side, the question goes to Krishna, and his answer is not the obvious one. Not Arjuna.

Not Bhima. Yudhishthira: the eldest brother, the one who lost everything at dice, the one Karna sent back to camp humiliated just the day before. Shalya is strong, Krishna says, in effect, and you are the one to meet him.
Put away your gentleness for today. And Yudhishthira, the man the epic keeps showing us as patient, picks up his weapons.

teach.b: The fight is long and fierce, and in Ganguli's English the patient king is almost unrecognizable: steady, fearless, pressing forward. At last Yudhishthira hurls a dart, a spear made for throwing, with all his strength.
It strikes Shalya, and the king of Madra falls. The twins have lost their uncle. As Shalya's army breaks, another fight finishes something older.
Shakuni, Duryodhana's uncle, the man who threw the dice in the rigged game, is still on the field.

In the dice hall, years before, the youngest brother Sahadeva had sworn that Shakuni would die by his hand. Now Sahadeva finds him. The dice-master has no dice here, and the vow from that hall is kept.
Twelve years in the forest, a year in hiding, eighteen days of war, and the wrong done at a gaming table is finally answered. Many Hindus hear a teaching in a day like this.

In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says: whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back in its place. Notice what that promises, and what it doesn't.
Not that wrong never wins: Shakuni won, for years.

teach.h: WRONG DOESN'T GET THE LAST WORD
teach.b: Only that it doesn't get the last word. Hindus hold on to that when cheating seems to pay. Dharma is restored, in its own time, not always in ours.
And Duryodhana, looking around, finds himself almost alone.

how: Yudhishthira's battle with Shalya and Sahadeva's killing of Shakuni are told in the Shalya Parva and in retellings and serials of the Mahabharata, as the moment the war's last vows begin to be kept.

o: the commander who falls to the patient eldest brother's dart
the dice-master Sahadeva had sworn to kill
the Pandava twin who keeps his vow from the dice hall

games.q: the last commander — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna chose Arjuna to fight Shalya
he chose Yudhishthira, the patient eldest brother.
Sahadeva's killing of Shakuni kept a vow from the dice hall
he had sworn there that Shakuni would die by his hand.
in the Gita, Krishna promises that wrong will never win, even for a while
he promises to come whenever dharma declines and set it back in place: restored, not never threatened.

games.q: a kid at school cheats all semester and keeps getting away with it. by Krishna's promise in the Gita, what fits?
o: keep doing right; dharma is restored in its time, and you do your part.
start cheating too; clearly dharma isn't coming.
spend the semester plotting his downfall.
games.why: Shakuni's rigged win held for years and still didn't get the last word. the Gita's promise is that dharma comes back; your part is to keep it meanwhile.

practice: Sit tall and let your face soften. Bring to mind one wrong that seems to be winning, in your life or in the news, and don't rehearse the anger.

If you pray, hand it to God, the way Hindus lean on Krishna's promise, and ask for patience and for the part that's yours to do. If you don't pray, name one small thing you can do for what's right, and leave the rest for now.

wordCard.voice: Shalya. The commander who falls to the patient eldest brother, while Sahadeva settles an old vow with the dice-master Shakuni.

orig.note: Yudhishthira: the eldest Pandava, who meets Shalya in battle.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma is restored, in its own time. The quiet brother remembered. See you tomorrow.
